what_it_does: Retrieval-augmented language models (RALMs) — AI assistants that look facts up in a database before answering — spend a lot of time and energy copying large amounts of data back and forth between memory chips and the processor that searches through them. This paper proposes Rimast, an architecture that instead does the searching directly inside a stack of memory chips (called 3D-stacked processing-in-memory, where thin compute logic is layered on top of dense memory), so most data never has to travel at all. The software side arranges stored data to avoid traffic jams (skew-free mapping) and decides dynamically which retrieval tasks to send into the memory versus keeping on the main chip. The abstract suggests this cuts data movement and speeds up retrieval, though exact numbers are not available here.
